title.en: The Great Yü Drains the Flood: The Mihist Hero-Model (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 大禹治水：墨者之榜樣（莊子）

region.en: The nine divisions of the drained empire (symbolic pin: Yuzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 九洲通流之地（象徵定位：河南禹州）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 33, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 33

summary.en: Mih Tzŭ's followers take for their model the Great Yü, who drained off the flood of waters, causing rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire — three hundred great rivers, three thousand branches, and streams without number. With his own hands he plied the bucket and dredger until his calves and shins had no hair left upon them; the wind bathed him, the rain combed him — and ages of Mihists wear short serge jackets and straw sandals, toil day and night, and make self-mortification their end and aim.
summary.zh: 昔者大禹湮洪水，疏九河，瀹濟漯而注諸海——腓無胈，脛無毛；沐甚雨，櫛疾風，置萬國。後世之墨者，多以裘褐為衣，以跂蹻為服，日夜不休，以自苦為極。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Mihist retelling of Yü's flood-labour within Zhuangzi's survey chapter, cross-linked to the flood cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Mih Tzŭ argued in favour of his system as follows:--Of old, the great Yü drained off the flood of waters, and caused rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire and the parts adjacent thereto,--three hundred great rivers, three thousand branches, and streams without number. With his own hands he plied the bucket and dredger, in order to reduce confusion to uniformity, until his calves and shins had no hair left upon them. The wind bathed him, the rain combed him; but he marked out the nations of the world, and was in very truth a Sage.

And because he thus sacrificed himself to the commonwealth, ages of Mihists to come would also wear short serge jackets and straw sandals, and toil day and night without stopping, making self-mortification their end and aim, and say to themselves, "If we cannot do this, we do not follow the TAO of Yü, and are unworthy to be called Mihists."

title.en: Hui Tzŭ's Ten Paradoxes: Feathers in an Egg, a Nail with a Tail (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 惠施多方，其書五車（莊子）

region.en: The schools of Sung and Liang (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋梁之辯（象徵定位：河南商丘）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 33, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 33

summary.en: Chuang Tzŭ's survey of Hui Tzŭ, whose learning filled five carts: the sun at noon is the sun setting; southwards there is no limit and yet there is a limit; one can reach Yüeh to-day and yet be there before; the middle of the world is north of Yen and south of Yüeh; there are feathers in an egg; a nail has a tail; fire is not hot; wheels do not press down the ground; the shadow of a flying bird does not move — a great philosopher and very subtle dialectician.
summary.zh: 惠施多方，其書五車；歷物之意曰：至大無外，謂之大一；至小無內，謂之小一——卵有毛；雞三足；郢有天下；犬可以為羊；馬有卵；丁子有尾；火不熱；目不見。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: That the sun at noon is the sun setting. That when an animal is born, it dies. That the likeness of things partly unlike is called the lesser likeness of unlikes. That the likeness of things altogether unlike is called the greater likeness of unlikes. That southwards there is no limit, and yet there is a limit. That one can reach Yüeh to-day and yet be there before. That joined rings can be separated. That the middle of the world is north of Yen and south of Yüeh.

He said that there were feathers in an egg. That a fowl had three feet. That Ying was the world. That a dog could be a sheep. That a mare could lay eggs. That a nail has a tail. That fire is not hot. That mountains have mouths. That wheels do not press down the ground. That the eye does not see. That the finger does not touch. That the uttermost extreme is not the end. That a tortoise is longer than a snake. That a carpenter's square is not square. That compasses will not make a circle. That the shadow of a flying bird does not move. That there is a moment when a swiftly-flying arrow is neither moving nor at rest. That a dog is not a hound. That a bay horse and a dun cow are three.
